extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys) involved in prosecution and enablement/best-mode analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification enables the full scope of the claimed invention and satisfies the best mode requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a)), including use of prior art, affidavits, burden of proof, and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit evidence probative and contemporaneous
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual evidence directed to the amount of time and effort and level of knowledge required for the practice of the invention from the disclosure, and knowledge in the art can be expected to rebut a prima facie case of nonenablement, but not opinion evidence directed to the ultimate legal question of enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits must be probative of the level of skill of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the time the applicant filed the application; affidavits stating what was known only at their execution date (not at filing) are insufficient (In re Gunn, In re Brown, Hirschfield). An affidavit showing an affiant was able to generate a program after being told the problem does not demonstrate that the application alone would have taught a POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art references must show usable, integrated guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely citing excerpts from technical publications or prior-art systems is not sufficient unless it is made clear that a person skilled in the art would know which parts could be used and how they could be interconnected to produce the required results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial availability of an identified prior-art computer system is pertinent but may not suffice. Prior art patents/publications relied upon must have publication dates earlier than the application's effective filing date (In re Budnick); patents issued after the filing date are not evidence of the knowledge of POSITA (In re Gunn). Applicants relying on prior art must show integration (set forth how prior-art components interconnect) to avoid undue experimentation (In re Scarbrough). When citing known programming techniques, the known and disclosed programming must be of approximately the same degree of complexity to demonstrate enablement (In re Knowlton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments of counsel cannot substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments of counsel alone cannot take the place of evidence in the record once an examiner has advanced a reasonable basis for questioning the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the record consists substantially of attorney arguments/opinions, the court expects factual affidavits or other evidence on enablement. Examiners should require evidentiary support rather than rely on counsel's statements (see In re Budnick, In re Schulze, In re Cole, In re Knowlton, In re Wiseman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between utility (35 U.S.C. 101) and enablement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as to how to use the invention is different from the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101: 101 requires some specific, substantial, and credible use; 112(a) requires an indication of how the use can be carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections based on lack of utility (101) should be imposed separately from enablement (112(a)) rejections when grounds differ. If a claim is nonuseful or inoperative (101), it necessarily fails the how-to-use aspect of enablement and both rejections should be made. Examiners should not maintain a 112(a) rejection grounded on lack of utility unless a proper 101 rejection exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden and applicant rebuttal for asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner has the initial burden of challenging an asserted utility; once the examiner shows a POSITA would reasonably doubt the asserted utility, the burden shifts to the applicant to provide rebuttal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fixed quantity or character of evidence required from the applicant; the amount and character will vary with what is claimed and how contrary the asserted utility is to established principles. The applicant's evidence need only make the asserted utility 'more likely than not' (not 'beyond a reasonable doubt'). Applicable cases include In re Fisher, In re Swartz, In re Brana, In re Bundy, In re Oetiker, In re Irons, and MPEP §2107 references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims (use Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: All questions of enablement are evaluated against the claimed subject matter; examiners will use the Wands factors to ascertain whether the amount of experimentation required to enable the full scope of the claimed invention is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine exactly what subject matter is encompassed by each claim (claims construed as a whole, dependent claims incorporate limitations). Examiner should identify any claimed subject matter not enabled and explain why, applying the Wands factors and citing unresolved questions that raise doubt. Enabling disclosure may be by specific example or broad terminology; the specification must teach how to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation (Amgen v. Sanofi, McRO, Wyeth & Cordis, Enzo Life Sciences, Idenix, In re Wright, In re Buchner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranges and genus claims require reasonable enablement across claimed scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When a range is claimed, there must be reasonable enablement of the scope of the range; a specification that warns against higher values within a claimed range suggests those values may not work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the disclosure reasonably enables the claimed range or genus. Case examples: AK Steel, Sanofi-Aventisub, In re Fisher, Amgen v. Chugai (EPO analogs), In re Goodman, In re Vaeck, Pac. Biosciences v. Oxford Nanopore. Broad claims that lack adequate disclosure for many embodiments may be rejected for lack of enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single means claim vulnerability to enablement rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A single means claim (means-plus-function recitation not in combination with another recited element) is subject to an enablement rejection if it covers every conceivable means for achieving the stated purpose while the specification discloses at most only those means known to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply In re Hyatt: if the claim covers all conceivable means but specification discloses few, rejection is appropriate. Similarly, claims reciting only a property/result that cover every structure accomplishing it may be nonenabling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling inoperative embodiments within claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of inoperative embodiments within the scope of a claim does not necessarily render the claim nonenabled; the standard is whether a skilled person could determine which embodiments would be inoperative or operative with no more effort than is normally required in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prophetic examples do not per se make disclosure nonenabling (Atlas Powder). However, where claims encompass significant numbers of inoperative embodiments and the specification fails to identify operable embodiments, requiring undue experimentation to find operable ones, a 112(a) enablement rejection is appropriate (Atlas Powder, In re Cook, In re Angstadt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclaimed feature taught as critical -> enablement rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A feature which is taught as critical in a specification and is not recited in the claims should result in a rejection under the enablement provision of 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine criticality by considering the entire disclosure; merely 'preferred' features are not 'critical' (In re Goffe). Only make such a rejection when the specification's language makes clear the limitation is critical for the invention to function. Broad language in the disclosure tends to rebut criticality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement — two-prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out the invention; compliance requires (1) a subjective inquiry whether the inventor possessed a best mode at filing, and (2) an objective inquiry whether the written description disclosed the best mode so a person skilled in the art could practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All applicants must disclose the best mode contemplated for the claimed subject matter even if the inventor is not the discoverer. Failure to disclose the best mode need not be active concealment. Case references: In re Nelson, Eli Lilly v. Barr, Benger Labs. Note: AIA (post-September 16, 2011) amended 35 U.S.C. 282 so failure to disclose best mode is not a defense to invalidate a patent, but the USPTO still examines best mode during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode practical considerations (examples, designation, updating, new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no statutory requirement to disclose a specific working example, to designate which embodiment is the best, or to update the best mode across priority filings; however, failure to disclose the best mode at filing cannot be cured by later-added new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best mode may be shown by a preferred range or group of reactants (In re Honn). No need to label an embodiment as 'best'. Updating best mode is not required for foreign priority or earlier-filed applications. Adding a specific mode later that was the inventor's best mode at filing is new matter and should be objected to (In re Hay). Consult supervisors if an earlier-filed application appears not to disclose the best mode and the earlier filing date is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode and enablement are separate requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The best mode provision of 35 U.S.C. 112 is a separate and distinct requirement from the enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to set forth any mode at all is effectively a nonenablement issue, but best mode focuses on concealing a preferred way to practice the claimed invention. See In re Newton and related authorities.
